data.name: Relic Keepers
data.detailed_description:
Sworn as a protector of the realm, your duty is protect a powerful relic hidden away in a small outpost. Suddenly, you hear a war horn as monsters rush in to attack the villagers and lay claim to the relic. Armed with your battle hardened sword, defend the villages and protect the relic against these vile intruders.

Relic keeper is an action game set in a fantasy setting. Helped by the village guards, keep the artefact safely inside the village walls and try to outlast against waves of evil creatures.

Features


  • An action game mixed with base defence gameplay.
  • Adapt yourself to different settings (Village, Desert Camp)
  • Battle hordes of vicious enemies
  • Defend your honor as you protect an important relic that will change the world
  • Visit multiple worlds and protect them from the horrors that infest them

reviews.review:
Relic Keepers is a compact fantasy action game that combines straightforward melee combat with wave-based objective defense. Developed and published by Idea Cabin, it casts the player as the guardian of an important relic threatened by invading monsters. The premise is immediately understandable: when the warning horn signals another attack, hostile creatures advance toward the settlement, and the player must prevent them from reaching what they came to destroy or capture. Rather than building an elaborate story around this responsibility, the game uses the relic as a practical reason for its repeated battles, keeping the emphasis firmly on combat and survival.

The main attraction is the combination of fighting enemies personally while protecting a fixed objective. Armed with a sword, the player confronts incoming creatures alongside guards who help defend the settlement. Having allies on the battlefield makes the encounters feel more like a desperate defensive stand than a conventional series of isolated fights. Positioning matters because simply defeating whatever happens to be nearby is not always enough; enemies moving toward the relic represent the greater threat. This creates a modest tactical element as the player decides where attention is most urgently required.

Its wave-oriented structure is both one of its strengths and its biggest limitations. There is an immediate satisfaction to seeing another assault approaching and attempting to stop the attackers before they overwhelm the defenses. The format also makes Relic Keepers easy to understand without requiring extensive preparation or complicated systems. Unfortunately, simplicity can quickly become repetition. A wave-defense game needs substantial enemy variety, escalating challenges, strong combat feedback, interesting progression, or changing tactical situations to remain compelling. Relic Keepers offers the foundation of that formula but does not develop it enough to provide the depth expected from stronger examples of the genre.

Different environments help provide some visual variation. The game takes its defensive battles beyond a single location, including settings such as a village and desert camp while presenting the broader idea of protecting different worlds from invading horrors. Moving between environments gives the adventure a greater sense of scale than defending the exact same arena indefinitely. Even so, these locations do not transform the fundamental experience. The focus remains on meeting waves of enemies with direct melee attacks while keeping them away from the objective.

Combat adopts a rough and violent fantasy style, including gore that makes the encounters more aggressive than the relatively simple visual presentation might initially suggest. Sword fighting is central to the experience, so enjoyment depends heavily on whether the basic act of repeatedly engaging enemies remains satisfying. Players expecting sophisticated combos, extensive equipment management, intricate character builds, or highly technical action mechanics may be disappointed. The combat is better approached as accessible wave-survival action rather than a deep hack-and-slash system.

The narrative is similarly restrained. The idea that the protected relic has enough importance to affect the world gives the player's mission some context, but storytelling is primarily there to establish the scenario rather than drive the experience. There is little reason to approach the game for elaborate characterization or a lengthy fantasy plot. Its strongest narrative quality is simply the atmosphere of being a lone central warrior supported by guards while increasingly dangerous creatures threaten an important location.

Relic Keepers is also distinctly small in overall scope. Its single-player focus means there is no dependency on finding an active multiplayer community, which is useful for an older and relatively obscure indie title. Steam achievements are included, although the very small achievement selection further reflects the modest amount of content. The game is therefore better suited to shorter sessions or players interested in exploring unusual independent projects than those looking for a lengthy action adventure filled with progression systems and extensive replay incentives.

Steam Deck compatibility requires some qualification. Relic Keepers does not have an official Steam Deck Verified or Playable rating displayed as a definitive compatibility classification. The game does have Linux and SteamOS support, which is encouraging for running it on Valve's handheld, but native platform support alone does not guarantee an ideal Steam Deck experience. Players should therefore regard its Deck status as officially unverified rather than assume complete compatibility. Controls, interface readability, performance, and other handheld-specific behavior may require individual testing.

The greatest issue is ultimately the difference between the potential of the concept and the depth of its execution. Defending a powerful artifact alongside guards while hordes descend upon different settlements could support an engaging mixture of action and defensive strategy. More substantial progression, stronger enemy differentiation, deeper combat mechanics, additional defensive options, and greater encounter variety could have made the formula considerably more memorable. Instead, the experience remains mechanically modest, and repetition becomes difficult to ignore.

As an obscure independent action game, Relic Keepers has some curiosity value. Its uncomplicated objectives, fantasy atmosphere, sword-based fighting, allied defenders, changing locations, and relentless monster attacks form a coherent experience, but they never develop into something particularly sophisticated. Players who enjoy discovering small experimental titles may appreciate its straightforward approach for a while, whereas anyone seeking polished combat or extensive strategic depth will probably find it lacking. It presents a workable foundation for a defensive fantasy action game but ultimately feels more like a limited interpretation of an interesting idea than a fully realized version of it.

Rating: 3/10
